subject: mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 8 periods = 320 minutes
Total: 8 periods · 5h 20min

section_titles: Different Units but Same Measure (kg and g)
periods.activity_title: Are These Weights Right? Scales and the kg–g Link

tasks_in_class.description: Tick the items from Anu's list whose recorded weights look correct (almirah 40g, bed 60kg, rice bag 5kg, sofa 30g, bucket 1kg800g, water bottle 650g, refrigerator 50g).
Read six dial weighing scales (a–f) showing different weights and write the correct weight for each.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Different Units but Same Measure, p.105
tasks_in_class.description: Match bags on Weighing Balance 1 (kg) with equivalent bags on Weighing Balance 2 (g), then fill in missing values on the double number line (kg and g).

time_bands.activity: Pose Anu's household list to the class. Students work in pairs on Check! Check!, p.104 ("Tick the items … weight look correct...."), discussing which entries seem wrong and why — gram vs kilogram for large furniture is the central tension. Draw out reasoning about familiar objects before confirming.

Display or project the six dial scales from Let Us Do, p.104 ("Read six dial weighing scales (a–f)...."). Walk students through reading the first scale together, noting how subdivisions are counted; students complete the remaining five independently and share answers.

Introduce the two-balance picture from Different Units but Same Measure, p.105 ("Match bags on Weighing Balance 1 (kg) with equivalent bags...."). Students match bags, then complete the double number line, discovering the ×1,000 relationship between kg and g through the pattern they see.

periods.teacher_notes: Students commonly confuse grams and kilograms for large objects — an almirah recorded as 40 g is the chapter's opening provocation, so let disagreement surface before resolving it. When reading scales, highlight that each scale's subdivisions must be counted from its own zero before reading a value. The double number line in the balances activity is the chapter's key representational tool; spend enough time here so students can articulate why 1 kg equals 1,000 g from the pattern, not merely as a stated fact.
materials: Blank double-number-line strips or whiteboard space

periods.activity_title: Who Is Right? Converting and Comparing Compound Weights

tasks_in_class.description: Decide who is correct about 5 kg 50 g in grams — Shamim (5,050 g) or Rehan (5,500 g) — and explain why.
Complete the double number line and fill in 6 conversions: (a) 7kg67g=___g (b) 3kg300g=___g (c) 8kg69g=___g (d) 10,760g=___kg___g (e) 4,080g=___kg___g (f) 12,042g=___kg___g.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Comparison between Different Weights Q2(a–f), p.107
tasks_in_class.description: Compare weight pairs using <, =, > signs: (a) 1kg600g vs 1,700g (b) 1kg600g vs 1kg60g (c) 10kg35g vs 10035g (d) 1kg600g vs 2kg500g (e) 5kg50g vs 4kg500g (f) 900g+7,000g vs 7kg+900g.

homework.book_ref: Comparison between Different Weights Q1(a)(b)(c), p.107
homework.description: From the picnic fruit list, identify (a) highest weight, (b) least weight, (c) arrange fruits in descending order of weight.

time_bands.activity: Present the Shamim–Rehan disagreement from Let Us Find Q1, p.106 ("Decide who is correct about 5 kg 50 g in grams...."). Students write their verdict and reasoning individually, then share in pairs, surfacing the common error of treating 50 g as 500 g before the class agrees on 5,050 g.

Students work through Let Us Find Q2, p.106 ("Complete the double number line and fill in 6 conversions...."), completing the number line first and using it as a scaffold for each fill-in item. Pairs cross-check answers, paying attention to items (d)–(f) where converting from grams back to kg+g requires careful division.

Introduce the strategy of converting to a common unit for comparison using Comparison between Different Weights Q2(a–f), p.107 ("Compare weight pairs using <, =, > signs...."). Work item (f) together (900g+7,000g vs 7kg+900g) as a class, then students complete the rest; discuss any disagreements. Homework noted in teacher notes below.

periods.teacher_notes: The most persistent error here is writing 5 kg 50 g as 5,500 g — treating the g digit-group as if it always occupies three full hundreds places. Let students articulate the correct reasoning (50 g stays as 50, not 500) before moving on. For comparison items, insist on converting both quantities to the same unit before placing the sign; item (f) involving a sum on each side often trips students who compare only the first number they see.

periods.activity_title: The Tiniest Grain: Milligrams, Quintals and Tonnes

tasks_in_class.description: If a sugar sachet weighs 5 g, how much is it in milligrams?
Complete the double number line relating g and mg with missing values.
Compare weight pairs using <, =, > signs: (a) 20g vs 200mg (b) 16g50mg vs 50g16mg (c) 2,010mg vs 2g100mg (d) 9,000mg vs 90g (e) 5,000g vs 7,500g (f) 800mg+88mg vs 880mg+8mg.
King donates wheat = 10× his weight. (a) If he donates 800 kg, what is his weight? (b) If he donated 780 kg last year, what was last year's weight? (c) How much weight did he gain this year?

homework.description: An ornament weighs 4 g 100 mg. What is its weight in milligrams?

time_bands.activity: Anchor the milligram through the ant and medicine context from the chapter. Pose Let Us Find Q1, p.108 ("If a sugar sachet weighs 5 g, how much is it in milligrams?") as an entry question; students estimate before computing, using the analogy that grams relate to kilograms in the same way milligrams relate to grams.

Students complete the g–mg double number line from Let Us Find Q2, p.108 ("Complete the double number line relating g and mg...."), mirroring how the kg–g line was built. Pairs share their completed lines, explaining each step, to establish the ×1,000 relationship between g and mg.

Students work through Let Us Find Q5(a–f), p.109 ("Compare weight pairs using <, =, > signs...."), converting to a single unit before comparing; item (f) involves a sum on each side and is done together as a class. Introduce quintals and tonnes briefly using the unit hierarchy panel in the text.

Students tackle King's Weight (a)(b)(c), p.109 ("King donates wheat = 10× his weight...."), reversing the ×10 operation to find the king's weight in (a), then finding last year's weight in (b), and subtracting in (c). Discuss as a class how dividing by 10 reverses the donation rule.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often assume that because 1 g = 1,000 mg mirrors 1 kg = 1,000 g, they can apply the same conversion process — this is correct and should be made explicit as a structural parallel. A common error in comparison items is ignoring the g component when the mg value looks large; insist on full conversion before comparison. For the King's Weight puzzle, guide students to identify division as the inverse of the ×10 donation rule before they compute.
materials: Small sugar sachets or medicine packets for referent sense (optional)

section_titles: From Tiny to Big — The Full Unit Hierarchy
The Grocery Store — Adding and Subtracting Weights
periods.activity_title: The Full Weight Chain: Adding and Subtracting at the Grocery Store

tasks_in_class.description: A restaurant owner uses 5kg200g, 8kg900g, and 12kg600g of onions over 3 days. Find the total weight.
4kg500g of sand is used from a 10kg sack. How much sand is left?
65kg flour purchased; 42kg275g used for langar; next day 52kg500g bought. What is the total flour now available?

homework.description: A rice sack weighs 9kg750g. After use it weighs 3kg700g. How much rice was used?

time_bands.activity: Display the unit hierarchy panel (mg → g → kg → quintal → tonne) from the chapter's summary section and read it together as a class. Students copy the chain into their notebooks and write two facts in their own words — this consolidates the complete weight unit structure before operations begin.

Model Rathna's grocery addition (2 kg 500 g + 1 kg 750 g) on the board using all three strategies described in the text: oral decomposition, column addition, and conversion to grams. Then students work Let Us Do Q1, p.111 ("A restaurant owner uses 5kg200g, 8kg900g, and 12kg600g...."), choosing any strategy and comparing methods with a partner.

Model regrouping in subtraction using the Rathna example (2 kg 500 g − 1 kg 750 g), showing that 1 kg is renamed as 1,000 g when the g column is insufficient. Students then solve Let Us Do Q3, p.111 ("4kg500g of sand is used from a 10kg sack...."), noting that 10 kg has 0 g and requires a full kilogram to be regrouped.

Students work the multi-step Gurdwara problem Let Us Do Q7, p.111 ("65kg flour purchased; 42kg275g used for langar; next day 52kg500g bought...."). Students plan the sequence of operations in writing before computing, then share their plans with the class.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently forget to regroup when the grams column in a subtraction is insufficient — make the renaming (1 kg → 1,000 g) explicit with a column layout on the board. The Gurdwara problem requires a subtraction followed by an addition; students who rush may add all three quantities instead of first subtracting the used flour. Additional practice on addition and subtraction: Let Us Do Q2, Q5, Q6 (p.111) may be used as seatwork or homework.

section_titles: More Operations on Weight — Multiplication and Division
periods.activity_title: Multiplying and Dividing Compound Weights: Grocery Costs

tasks_in_class.description: Find total cost of grocery items: rice 12kg500g @₹60/kg, flour 7kg250g @₹40/kg, sugar 5kg @₹45/kg, chana dal 3kg600g @₹70/kg, besan 4kg @₹60/kg, jaggery 1kg400g @₹50/kg.
A box of nuts (4kg800g) is equally distributed into 4 boxes. What is the weight of each box in grams?
4 people need 500g rice. How much rice for 8 people? Use the double number line (×2 scaling).
Nitesh (scrap dealer): (a) cost of 16kg newspaper @₹8/kg; (b) cost of 20kg iron @₹200/10kg; (c) cost of 10kg plastic @₹30/5kg. Make double number lines for (b) and (c).

time_bands.activity: Use the text's modelled example (4 × 10 kg 500 g) to demonstrate distributing multiplication over kg and g on the board, and the alternative of converting to grams first. Students discuss which approach suits which numbers; establish both methods as valid before students tackle their own work.

Students work through Let Us Do Q1, p.112 ("Find total cost of grocery items: rice 12kg500g @₹60/kg...."), converting fractional-kg quantities to grams or decimals before multiplying by the per-kg price; they work in small groups, each group responsible for two items, then combine to find the total bill.

Model division of compound weight (4 kg 800 g ÷ 4) using both splitting-by-column and convert-to-grams methods. Students solve Let Us Do Q2, p.112 ("A box of nuts (4kg800g) is equally distributed into 4 boxes....") and immediately connect it to the scaling task Let Us Do Q2 (scaling), p.112 ("4 people need 500g rice. How much rice for 8 people?"), completing the double number line.

Students work Let Us Do Q4(a)(b)(c), p.113 ("Nitesh (scrap dealer): (a) cost of 16kg newspaper...."), drawing double number lines for (b) and (c) to read the cost per target quantity by scaling; discuss as a class how the number line makes the proportional step visible.

periods.teacher_notes: A common error in the grocery cost table is treating 12 kg 500 g as 12.5 kg but then forgetting to halve the per-kg price for the 500 g portion; having students write out the split (12 kg at ₹60 = ₹720; 500 g = half kg at ₹30) prevents this. For division problems, students who divide kg and g separately sometimes get stuck when the g column does not divide evenly — guide them to convert the remainder kilograms to grams and continue dividing.
materials: Whiteboard for multiplication and division modelling

section_titles: Measuring Capacity — Introducing Litres and Millilitres
Big to Small, Small to Big — l and ml Conversion
Different Units but Same Measure — l and ml Double Number Line
periods.activity_title: From Tea Cups to Milk Deliveries: Litres, Millilitres and Conversions

tasks_in_class.description: Discuss: how much water and milk is needed for 2 cups of tea? Is 1 l too much, or is 500 ml enough?
A bucket can hold a maximum of 20 ml of water — is this correct? Which unit should be used?

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Big to Small, Small to Big Q2, p.113
tasks_in_class.description: Muskaan drinks 3 l of water a day. How many times must she refill a 500 ml bottle? How many ml does she drink?

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Different Units but Same Measure (milkman), p.114
tasks_in_class.description: Complete the double number line (l and ml) and fill the milkman's weekly delivery table converting between l and ml for five families.
Mary says 1l400ml = 1,400ml; Daisy says 1,040ml. Who is correct and why?

time_bands.activity: Open with the tea-making discussion from Measuring Capacity Q1, p.113 ("Discuss: how much water and milk is needed for 2 cups of tea?...."). Students give their estimates and reasons; follow immediately with Measuring Capacity Q2, p.113 ("A bucket can hold a maximum of 20 ml...."), using the absurdity of 20 ml to establish litre as the appropriate unit for large containers.

Students solve Big to Small, Small to Big Q2, p.113 ("Muskaan drinks 3 l of water a day. How many times must she refill a 500 ml bottle?...."), recording the repeated addition (500+500+…=3,000 ml) and connecting it to the 1,000 ml = 1 l equivalence. Briefly extend: note T-30 (Ramiz's bottles) as additional practice on the same conversion idea, assignable as seatwork.

Students complete the l–ml double number line and milkman's weekly delivery table from Different Units but Same Measure (milkman), p.114 ("Complete the double number line (l and ml) and fill the milkman's weekly delivery table...."), mirroring the kg–g double number line they worked with earlier in the chapter.

Present the Mary–Daisy disagreement from Let Us Think Q1, p.115 ("Mary says 1l400ml = 1,400ml; Daisy says 1,040ml. Who is correct?"). Students write their verdict and explanation before a class vote; use the wrong answer (1,040 ml) to surface the place-value misconception. Assign Let Us Think Q2(a–f) as homework.

periods.teacher_notes: The capacity sections parallel the weight sections structurally — students who understood kg↔g conversion should find l↔ml transfer relatively smooth, so make the parallel explicit. The error mirrored by Daisy (1 l 400 ml = 1,040 ml) is the same place-value confusion as Rehan's 5 kg 50 g = 5,500 g in the weight section; naming this connection helps students self-monitor. Additional practice on reading pictorial containers: Big to Small, Small to Big Q3 (p.114) may be used as seatwork.

section_titles: Let Us Compare — Petrol Pump; Adding and Subtracting Capacity
periods.activity_title: Petrol Pump Problems: Comparing, Adding and Subtracting Capacity

tasks_in_class.description: Fill total fuel per vehicle type in table; (a) how much more fuel for buses than trucks? (b) total fuel from pump on that day?
Compare capacity pairs using <, =, >: (a) 5l600ml vs 5,400ml (b) 10l100ml vs 1l600ml (c) 190ml+800ml vs 800ml+109ml (d) 3l600ml vs 3,600ml (e) 4l50ml vs 4l500ml.
Tina bought 2l500ml petrol; Sam bought 2l800ml more than Tina. How much petrol did Sam buy?

time_bands.activity: Students study the petrol pump table and work Let Us Compare Q2(a)(b), p.116 ("Fill total fuel per vehicle type in table; (a) how much more fuel for buses than trucks?...."). Pairs compute totals per vehicle type by multiplication first, then subtract for (a) and add all types for (b); share strategies.

Students work Let Us Compare Q3(a–e), p.116 ("Compare capacity pairs using <, =, >...."), converting each side to ml before placing the sign. Item (c) requires adding the two ml quantities on each side and item (e) targets the 4 l 50 ml vs 4 l 500 ml confusion; these are done together on the board.

Model column addition of l+ml (including regrouping 1,300 ml → 1 l 300 ml) and column subtraction with regrouping (1 l → 1,000 ml) using examples from the text. Students solve Let Us Compare Q4, p.116 ("Tina bought 2l500ml petrol; Sam bought 2l800ml more than Tina...."), then discuss why the ml column sum exceeds 1,000 and how to carry.

periods.teacher_notes: Students working the petrol pump table may try to add across vehicle types before multiplying by quantity per vehicle — insist on the multiplication step first. In comparison item (e), 4 l 50 ml versus 4 l 500 ml is a deliberate trap for students who read the ml digit-by-digit rather than as a three-digit number; use it as a formative check. For addition and subtraction of l+ml, the regrouping rule is identical to that for kg+g and should be named as such.

section_titles: Let Us Solve — Multi-step Capacity Word Problems
periods.activity_title: Filling, Pouring, Dividing: Multi-step Capacity Challenges

tasks_in_class.description: Riya fills one 2l bottle + four 500ml bottles; Aarav fills three 750ml bottles. Who filled more? How much more?
Milk poured equally into 8 glasses (360ml each), 120ml left. (a) Total capacity of 8 glasses? (b) Initial milk in bottle? (c) Cost of 3l milk @₹40/l?
Juice vendor: 5l container, each glass 250ml. (a) How many full glasses? (b) After 10 glasses served, juice left? (c) Earnings selling 5l @₹25/250ml?
8l400ml of oil equally poured into 7 containers. How much oil per container?

homework.description: One container holds 1l75ml of buttermilk. How much buttermilk in 8 such containers?

time_bands.activity: Students read and plan Let Us Solve Q1, p.118 ("Riya fills one 2l bottle + four 500ml bottles; Aarav fills three 750ml bottles. Who filled more?....") in writing — listing each person's total before comparing. The plan step (write what each person fills, then add, then subtract) is made explicit before computing.

Students tackle Let Us Solve Q2(a)(b)(c), p.118 ("Milk poured equally into 8 glasses (360ml each), 120ml left...."), working sub-questions in sequence: (a) multiplication to find glass total, (b) addition to find original bottle, (c) unit conversion then cost. Groups share and reconcile their answers.

Students work Let Us Solve Q3(a)(b)(c), p.118 ("Juice vendor: 5l container, each glass 250ml...."), using the double number line as suggested in the text to find the glass count for (a), then subtraction for (b), and multiplication for (c). Discuss how the number line makes the division visible.

Students work Let Us Solve Q4, p.118 ("8l400ml of oil equally poured into 7 containers....") by converting to ml first (8,400 ml ÷ 7) then expressing the result back as l+ml. Let Us Solve Q5 is noted as homework. Bring the unit to a close by asking students to name one conversion rule they feel confident about — a brief oral share-round.

periods.teacher_notes: Multi-step problems are where students most often lose track of units — encourage writing the unit alongside every intermediate result, not just the final answer. For Q4, dividing 8,400 ml by 7 is straightforward but students must remember to convert back to l+ml; leaving the answer as 1,200 ml rather than 1 l 200 ml is a presentation error worth addressing. Q5 (multiplication of 1 l 75 ml by 8) is assigned as homework to give further practice with multiplying compound capacity quantities.

items.prompt: A shopkeeper writes the weight of a school bag as 2 g. Which statement best explains whether this is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: It is correct; a school bag is a small object so grams are the right unit.

options.label: B
options.text: It is not correct; a school bag is much heavier and should be recorded in kilograms, not grams.

options.label: C
options.text: It is correct; 2 g and 2 kg mean the same thing.

options.label: D
options.text: It is not correct; school bags cannot be weighed at all.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Option B — a school bag weighs several kilograms, so recording it as 2 g is unreasonable; kilograms are the appropriate unit.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare the recorded unit with the expected mass of a familiar everyday object to judge plausibility.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student thinks small-looking numbers in grams are always reasonable, without considering that 2 g is far too light for a bag.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student conflates grams and kilograms as interchangeable labels, not recognising the 1,000-fold difference.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student avoids the reasoning task by rejecting the premise, indicating unfamiliarity with measurement plausibility.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student hold a known 1 kg object to feel the referent; stretch: ask them to write a plausible weight range in kg for three other school items.

exercise.description: Tick the items from Anu's list whose recorded weights look correct (almirah 40g, bed 60kg, rice bag 5kg, sofa 30g, bucket 1kg800g, water bottle 650g, refrigerator 50g).

items.section_title: Different Units but Same Measure (kg and g)
items.prompt: A bag of flour shows 3 kg on one weighing balance. What will the other balance show if it reads in grams? Write the weight in grams and explain how you found it.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 3,000 g. Because 1 kg = 1,000 g, multiply 3 by 1,000 to get 3,000 g.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the relationship 1 kg = 1,000 g and multiply the kg value by 1,000.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: encourage the student to use the double number line to count up in thousands; stretch: ask what 3 kg 500 g would show on the grams balance.

exercise.book_ref: Different Units but Same Measure, p.105
exercise.description: Match bags on Weighing Balance 1 (kg) with equivalent bags on Weighing Balance 2 (g), then fill in missing values on the double number line (kg and g).

items.prompt: Priya says 4 kg 30 g equals 4,030 g. Ravi says it equals 4,300 g. Who is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Ravi is correct; 30 g becomes 300 g when you add it to kilograms.

options.label: B
options.text: Both are correct; you can write it either way.

options.label: C
options.text: Priya is correct; 4 kg = 4,000 g and adding 30 g gives 4,030 g.

options.label: D
options.text: Neither is correct; the answer is 430 g.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Priya is correct: 4 kg = 4,000 g, so 4 kg 30 g = 4,000 + 30 = 4,030 g.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Convert kg to g by multiplying by 1,000, then add the remaining grams.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student pads the grams value to fill three digit-places, treating 30 as 300 — the target misconception.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student does not recognise that only one converted value is mathematically correct.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student drops the thousands from the kg conversion entirely, showing a partial conversion error.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student write the conversion in two steps (4 kg = ___ g; ___ g + 30 g = ___); stretch: ask them to convert 4 kg 305 g and explain the difference.

exercise.description: Decide who is correct about 5 kg 50 g in grams — Shamim (5,050 g) or Rehan (5,500 g) — and explain why.

items.prompt: Which sign correctly completes this comparison? 2 kg 50 g ☐ 2,500 g

options.label: D
options.text: Cannot be compared because they use different units.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: < (less than). 2 kg 50 g = 2,050 g, which is less than 2,500 g.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Convert both quantities to grams (2 kg 50 g = 2,050 g) then compare the resulting numbers.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student may have read the 50 as 500 and concluded 2,500 g = 2,500 g.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student incorrectly treats 2 kg 50 g as larger, possibly reading '50' as '500' and getting 2,500 g, then adding instead of converting.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student does not apply the conversion strategy and treats mixed-unit quantities as incomparable.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: prompt the student to write 2 kg 50 g in grams using a two-step box (2 kg = ___ g; ___ g + 50 g = ___); stretch: ask them to write another pair where the same digit appears in different positions and leads to a different comparison result.

exercise.book_ref: Comparison between Different Weights Q2(a–f), p.107
exercise.description: Compare weight pairs using <, =, > signs: (a) 1kg600g vs 1,700g (b) 1kg600g vs 1kg60g (c) 10kg35g vs 10035g (d) 1kg600g vs 2kg500g (e) 5kg50g vs 4kg500g (f) 900g+7,000g vs 7kg+900g.

items.prompt: Which sign correctly completes this comparison? 3 g 20 mg ☐ 3,200 mg

options.label: D
options.text: Cannot be compared because mg and g are different units.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: < (less than). 3 g 20 mg = 3,020 mg, which is less than 3,200 mg.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Convert g to mg by multiplying by 1,000 and add the remaining mg, then compare the two numbers.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student likely treats 3 g 20 mg as 3,200 mg (padding 20 to 200) and then incorrectly judges it as larger.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student made the same padding error (20 → 200) and then concluded equality.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student does not apply the g-to-mg conversion strategy and treats mixed-unit quantities as incomparable.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student use the g–mg double number line to locate 3 g 20 mg; stretch: ask them to write two more mg vs g+mg pairs, one where the left side is greater and one where it is less.

exercise.description: Compare weight pairs using <, =, > signs: (a) 20g vs 200mg (b) 16g50mg vs 50g16mg (c) 2,010mg vs 2g100mg (d) 9,000mg vs 90g (e) 5,000g vs 7,500g (f) 800mg+88mg vs 880mg+8mg.

items.section_title: More Operations on Weight — Multiplication and Division
items.prompt: A recipe needs 300 g of lentils per person. If 6 people are eating, how much lentils is needed in all? Use a double number line to show your thinking.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 1,800 g. The double number line scales 300 g × 6 = 1,800 g (or equivalent skip-count: 300, 600, 900, 1,200, 1,500, 1,800).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply the per-person quantity by the number of people using the double number line as a proportional model.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student fill the number line tick by tick (300, 600, …) before reading the answer; stretch: ask how many people can be fed if 2,400 g of lentils are available.

exercise.description: 4 people need 500g rice. How much rice for 8 people? Use the double number line (×2 scaling).

items.section_title: Measuring Capacity — Introducing Litres and Millilitres
items.prompt: A large cooking pot holds 8 _____ of water. Which unit makes this sentence correct?

options.label: A
options.text: milligrams

options.label: B
options.text: millilitres

options.label: C
options.text: litres

options.label: D
options.text: grams

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Litres. A large cooking pot holds several litres; millilitres would make 8 ml far too small for a cooking pot.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare the size of the container to the referent size of each unit and choose the unit that gives a sensible number.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student confuses weight and capacity units or has no referent for milligrams.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student selects a capacity unit but underestimates the size of a cooking pot; 8 ml is a teaspoon-sized amount.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student confuses weight and capacity, picking a weight unit for a capacity context.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student whether they could drink 8 ml or 8 litres in one day and use that to build referent sense; stretch: ask them to suggest a sensible capacity for a drinking glass and for a water tank, with units.

exercise.description: Discuss: how much water and milk is needed for 2 cups of tea? Is 1 l too much, or is 500 ml enough?

items.section_title: Different Units but Same Measure — l and ml Double Number Line
items.prompt: Arjun says 2 l 60 ml = 2,060 ml. Sneha says it equals 2,600 ml. Who is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Sneha is correct; 60 ml becomes 600 ml when you add it to litres.

options.label: B
options.text: Arjun is correct; 2 l = 2,000 ml and adding 60 ml gives 2,060 ml.

options.label: C
options.text: Both are correct; the ml value can be written as either 60 or 600.

options.label: D
options.text: Neither is correct; the answer is 260 ml.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Arjun is correct: 2 l = 2,000 ml and 2,000 + 60 = 2,060 ml.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Convert litres to millilitres by multiplying by 1,000, then add the remaining millilitres.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student pads 60 ml to 600 ml to fill three digit-places — the same place-value misconception as Daisy's error in the chapter.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student does not recognise that only one numerical value is correct after conversion.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student drops the thousands entirely and adds 200 + 60 from the digits, showing a digit-concatenation error.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student write the conversion in two steps on a number line (2 l = ___ ml; ___ ml + 60 ml = ___); stretch: ask them to convert 2 l 605 ml and compare with 2,065 ml.

exercise.description: Mary says 1l400ml = 1,400ml; Daisy says 1,040ml. Who is correct and why?

items.section_title: Let Us Compare — Petrol Pump; Adding and Subtracting Capacity
items.prompt: Which sign correctly completes this comparison? 6 l 40 ml ☐ 6,400 ml

options.label: D
options.text: Cannot be compared; one is in mixed units and the other in ml.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: < (less than). 6 l 40 ml = 6,040 ml, which is less than 6,400 ml.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Convert 6 l 40 ml to ml (6,000 + 40 = 6,040 ml) and compare the two numbers directly.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student likely padded 40 ml to 400 ml and concluded 6,400 ml = 6,400 ml.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student padded 40 to 400, got 6,400 ml, and then judged left side as greater due to a further error.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student does not apply the conversion strategy and treats mixed-unit quantities as incomparable.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student convert 6 l 40 ml step by step in writing before comparing; stretch: ask them to find a ml value between 6 l 40 ml and 6,400 ml and express it in l+ml form.

exercise.description: Compare capacity pairs using <, =, >: (a) 5l600ml vs 5,400ml (b) 10l100ml vs 1l600ml (c) 190ml+800ml vs 800ml+109ml (d) 3l600ml vs 3,600ml (e) 4l50ml vs 4l500ml.

items.prompt: A weighing scale has markings at 0, 250 g, 500 g, 750 g, and 1,000 g. The pointer stops exactly halfway between 250 g and 500 g. What weight does the scale show?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Find the midpoint between adjacent scale markings by adding them and dividing by 2.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student may have added a fixed 50 g step above 250 g without reasoning about the midpoint.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student added 100 g above 250 g, treating the interval as a 200 g gap but halving incorrectly.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student added 150 g to 250 g, overshooting the midpoint by 25 g.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to count the gap from 250 to 500 (250 g) and then halve it (125 g) and add to 250; stretch: ask what the pointer shows if it is three-quarters of the way from 250 to 500.

exercise.description: Read six dial weighing scales (a–f) showing different weights and write the correct weight for each.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply the kg value by 1,000 to get grams, then add the remaining grams.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: offer the two-step scaffold (6 kg = ___ g; ___ + 9 = ___) on a slip of paper; stretch: ask the student to convert 6,090 g back to kg+g form and compare the two results.

exercise.description: Complete the double number line and fill in 6 conversions: (a) 7kg67g=___g (b) 3kg300g=___g (c) 8kg69g=___g (d) 10,760g=___kg___g (e) 4,080g=___kg___g (f) 12,042g=___kg___g.

items.section_title: Different Units but Same Measure — l and ml Double Number Line
items.prompt: A milkman delivers 5 l 7 ml of milk to one house. Write this amount in millilitres.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply the litre value by 1,000 to convert to ml, then add the remaining ml.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student use the l–ml double number line to locate 5 l then add 7 steps of 1 ml; stretch: ask the student to convert 5,070 ml back to l+ml form and explain the difference from 5,007 ml.

exercise.book_ref: Different Units but Same Measure (milkman), p.114
exercise.description: Complete the double number line (l and ml) and fill the milkman's weekly delivery table converting between l and ml for five families.

items.section_title: Different Units but Same Measure — l and ml Double Number Line

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply the litre value by 1,000 and add the remaining millilitres.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: prompt the student to write the conversion in two separate steps before combining; stretch: ask the student to convert 7,800 ml to l+ml and compare it with 7,080 ml to see how place value changes the meaning.

items.prompt: A king donates grain equal to 10 times his own weight each harvest. This harvest he donates 920 kg. What is the king's weight in kg?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 92 kg. Divide the donated amount by 10: 920 ÷ 10 = 92 kg.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide the donated quantity by 10 to reverse the multiplication and find the king's weight.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to check by multiplying their answer by 10 and seeing if it gives 920; stretch: ask how much more grain the king would donate if he gained 5 kg.

exercise.description: King donates wheat = 10× his weight. (a) If he donates 800 kg, what is his weight? (b) If he donated 780 kg last year, what was last year's weight? (c) How much weight did he gain this year?

items.section_title: The Grocery Store — Adding and Subtracting Weights
items.prompt: A school canteen bought 30 kg of rice. They used 18 kg 650 g for lunch and then bought 12 kg 500 g more. How much rice is available now?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Subtract the used weight from the original stock, then add the new purchase; regroup 1 kg as 1,000 g when the g column is insufficient.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: guide the student to write the two steps separately and check each with column layout; stretch: ask how many more grams of rice would be needed to reach exactly 25 kg.

exercise.description: 65kg flour purchased; 42kg275g used for langar; next day 52kg500g bought. What is the total flour now available?

items.section_title: More Operations on Weight — Multiplication and Division
items.prompt: A basket of apples weighing 6 kg 400 g is shared equally among 4 friends. What is each person's share in grams?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 1,600 g. Convert 6 kg 400 g to grams: 6,400 g. Then 6,400 ÷ 4 = 1,600 g.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Convert the compound weight to grams, then divide by the number of people.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: encourage the student to convert to grams first before dividing; stretch: ask the student to express the answer in kg+g form and check by multiplying 1 kg 600 g by 4.

exercise.description: A box of nuts (4kg800g) is equally distributed into 4 boxes. What is the weight of each box in grams?

items.section_title: Let Us Compare — Petrol Pump; Adding and Subtracting Capacity
items.prompt: A petrol pump fills cars and motorcycles in a morning. Cars take 15 l 500 ml each and motorcycles take 8 l 200 ml each. If 3 cars and 2 motorcycles are filled, how much petrol is used in total?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 63 l 100 ml. Cars: 3 × 15 l 500 ml = 46 l 500 ml. Motorcycles: 2 × 8 l 200 ml = 16 l 400 ml. Total: 46 l 500 ml + 16 l 400 ml = 62 l 900 ml.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply each vehicle type's quantity by its count, then add the two results, regrouping 1,000 ml as 1 l if needed.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to handle cars and motorcycles separately before adding; stretch: ask how much petrol remains if the pump started with 100 l.

exercise.description: Fill total fuel per vehicle type in table; (a) how much more fuel for buses than trucks? (b) total fuel from pump on that day?

items.section_title: Let Us Solve — Multi-step Capacity Word Problems
items.prompt: Deepa fills one 1 l 500 ml bottle and three 250 ml bottles with juice for a picnic. Her friend Kavya fills two 750 ml bottles. Who carried more juice, and by how much?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Deepa carried more. Deepa: 1,500 ml + 3 × 250 ml = 1,500 + 750 = 2,250 ml. Kavya: 2 × 750 ml = 1,500 ml. Difference: 2,250 − 1,500 = 750 ml.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Convert each person's bottles to ml, add within each person's total, then subtract the smaller total from the larger.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to list each bottle's ml value separately before adding; stretch: ask how many more 250 ml bottles Kavya would need to match Deepa exactly.

exercise.description: Riya fills one 2l bottle + four 500ml bottles; Aarav fills three 750ml bottles. Who filled more? How much more?

items.section_title: Let Us Solve — Multi-step Capacity Word Problems
items.prompt: A juice shop has a 5 l container. Each glass holds 200 ml. After serving 12 glasses, how much juice is left in the container?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 2,600 ml (or 2 l 600 ml). Juice served: 12 × 200 ml = 2,400 ml. Juice left: 5,000 − 2,400 = 2,600 ml.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply glasses by ml per glass to find juice served, then subtract from the starting amount converted to ml.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: encourage the student to convert 5 l to ml first, then subtract; stretch: ask how many more glasses can be served from what remains, and whether there is any juice left over.

exercise.description: Juice vendor: 5l container, each glass 250ml. (a) How many full glasses? (b) After 10 glasses served, juice left? (c) Earnings selling 5l @₹25/250ml?
